A follow-up attached to one response

The reference file on a checkbox field is unconditional: the technician sees it whatever they answer. A follow-up is the same content, text plus one optional file, tied to a single response and shown only when that response is given. The technician reads it on the card as an instruction; the builder calls it a follow-up, because that is what the author is adding. Acknowledgement is offered on
only, on by default, and the author can turn it off. Follow-ups on

are read-only and never need acknowledging. Where it is on, the inspection cannot be submitted until the technician has confirmed they read it. It carries no colour of its own. The blue already used for the reference file marks it as something to read, and the acknowledgement pill takes the colour of the response that triggered it, so red and amber keep meaning what they mean. Per axle fields do not carry follow-ups: a verdict there belongs to a position, and a follow-up would have no single position to sit on.

The author can see what a follow-up consists of before committing to one: a box of text and one file. The checkbox is the condition, and it only switches the two fields under it from off to on. Monitor and Not OK carry Require acknowledgement, on by default. OK and N/A have no acknowledgement toggle.

The checked block is the only one with a white ground and a blue edge. Its text area grows to four rows once it can be typed in, and Attach File is replaced by the file it took. Unchecking it keeps what was written until the field is saved, so a mis-click is not a loss.

With Include Monitor option off, the Monitor row and its whole block go: three responses, three blocks. Text written against Monitor is kept and comes back with the row, and Not OK keeps its own acknowledgement setting.

The cost is height: four blocks make the response list about 990 px instead of 280, which is why it sits behind a toggle that is off by default. Turning the toggle off again with one checked asks first, since there is text to lose. Include Monitor option sits beside it because both change which responses exist, not how one is validated. The two panels that hid the fields behind an Add Follow-up click are gone: neither showed the author what a follow-up is before they committed to making one, and neither carried the per-response acknowledgement toggle.

Applies to air-brake foundation assemblies on tractors and trailers.
Free stroke and applied stroke must both be measured with the system at full reservoir pressure. Chock the wheels and release the parking brake before beginning.
Air pressure at or above 90 psi. Engine off. Wheels chocked. Parking brake released and the transmission in neutral.
Mark the push rod where it leaves the chamber with the brakes fully released.
Using a lever, move the slack adjuster until the shoes contact the drum.
Measure between the mark and the chamber face. Free stroke should read between 3/8 in. and 5/8 in.
Have an assistant make a full brake application and hold it.
Measure the total travel of the push rod. Compare against the chamber size table on page 2.
Record both figures on the inspection. Travel beyond the readjustment limit is an out-of-service condition under FMCSA Appendix G.

Measure the outside diameter of the chamber to identify the type when the stamping is not legible. If the reading is within 1/8 in. of the limit, mark the position Monitor and note the figure so the next PM can compare.

Worn brake lining, a stretched or misaligned push rod, a seized automatic slack adjuster, or a chamber diaphragm that has begun to leak. Replace the adjuster rather than attempting to free a seized unit.

Enter both figures on the inspection against the axle and position measured. A position beyond the readjustment limit is Not OK, requires a note describing the cause, and requires a photograph of the assembly.

Under FMCSA Appendix G a vehicle is placed out of service when 20 percent or more of the brakes on the unit are defective. A single brake beyond the adjustment limit counts as defective for that calculation.
Re-check free stroke after any adjuster or chamber replacement, and again after a short road test.

A dual axle records four tire pressures, so it needs four verdicts. Each value carries its own: a dropdown attached to the input it judges, so left outer can be Not OK while left inner is OK. That grid is the whole record: no status column, no per-row legend, no axle roll-up badge, no counters. Colour lives on the value that earned it and on the control you press. A tire in the top view takes the worst verdict entered for it so far and stays grey until one arrives; nothing is ever auto-filled. Switching Single / Dual asks nothing; typed values come back if you switch back. Marking OK in bulk exists at three levels: the inspection row, the section row, and every field's own card header, whatever its type. Mark all OK, Mark section OK and Mark field OK are the same quiet action on the same right edge, so the level is read from the row it sits on rather than from the label. Each fills only what is still Not inspected, never overwrites a verdict already picked, and never writes a value.

# Conditional Follow-up V2.dc.html — visible text per page (hidden tooltip text excluded; it is listed per interaction)

The reference file on a checkbox field is unconditional: the technician sees it whatever they answer. A follow-up is the same content, text plus one optional file, tied to a single response and shown only when that response is given. The technician reads it on the card as an instruction; the builder calls it a follow-up, because that is what the author is adding. Acknowledgement is offered on Monitor and Not OK only, on by default, and the author can turn it off. Follow-ups on OK and N/A are read-only and never need acknowledging. Where it is on, the inspection cannot be submitted until the technician has confirmed they read it. It carries no colour of its own. The blue already used for the reference file marks it as something to read, and the acknowledgement pill takes the colour of the response that triggered it, so red and amber keep meaning what they mean. Per axle fields do not carry follow-ups: a verdict there belongs to a position, and a follow-up would have no single position to sit on.

The canvas row gains a short list: one line per follow-up, the response in its own colour, the first line of the text, and a clip where a file is attached. It sits on every field that has one, selected or not, so an author reviewing a long template reads what the template does without clicking through it field by field. Lines shorten; they do not wrap. Everything above the response list, and the general reference file and validation below it, are unchanged from TB3.
Before you touch the chamber, chock the wheels, cage the spring brake on that wheel end and drain the wet tank until the gauge reads zero. Do not crack the supply line while the system is charged.

Tag the unit out of service before it leaves the bay and tell the foreman in person, not over the radio. If the foreman is not on site, call the service advisor and write the time of the call in the note.

If the leak is at the push-rod seal rather than the clamp band, check the slack adjuster travel on the same wheel end and measure the lining at the same time, because a seal that has been weeping will usually have taken the shoe with it.

Replace the chamber as an assembly. Do not reuse the clamp band, the mounting nuts or the push-rod yoke pin, and torque the mounting nuts to the value on the axle decal, not the generic value in the manual.

Do not release the unit for road test until the replacement chamber is fitted, the system has held 90 psi for five minutes with the engine off, and the brake has been stroked ten times with no drop beyond the allowance in the attached procedure.

pages across Foundations (Logo, Colors, Typography, Icons, Effects, Spacing), Components (Avatar, Buttons, Checkboxes, Toggles, Inputs, Breadcrumbs, Badges, Headers, Tables, Modals, Tabs, Tooltip, Menus, Notifications, Side-Panel), plus Dara playground work exploring real product screens (Work Order, Schedule, Inventory, Finance).
Dashed purple** (`#7B61FF` / `#8A38F5`) is used *only* in design-system documentation to delineate component spec regions — never in product.
Fixed top bar + fixed side panel + scrollable content** is the dominant shell.
No hand-drawn illustrations or background patterns.** The surface vocabulary is clean: white, grey-25, and subtle tinted cards (warm `#FFFAEB` for help/guidance, cool `#E9F5FF` for tips).
No gradients** in product UI. Primary blue is a flat fill.
No photography** in the design system; product screens are text-and-data dense.
Data visualization** uses success/warning/error semantics for status chips in tables, and additional colors (teal, cyan, violet, pink) for distinct categories.
Hover = **color shift + subtle lift (shadow-sm → shadow-md)**, not scale.
Active/press = **darker fill + no shadow**, not shrink.
Loading buttons show a small row of pulsing circles in place of the label, preserving width.
No entrance animations on route changes.
Overlays behind modals: `rgba(15,17,26,0.5)`, no blur. (Shopview does not use frosted glass.)
Disabled buttons: reduce to ~40% opacity of their default state.
Shopview appears to ship as a single web application with distinct workspaces:
Secondary buttons invert the treatment: white bg, grey-300 border, grey-700 text; hover → grey-50 bg, grey-400 border.
Stroke style.** Line/outlined, not filled, not duotone.
No emoji in product UI.** Guideline docs may use ✅ ⚠️ ❌ to describe semantic meaning, but the UI never ships emoji as an icon.
No unicode glyphs as icons.** Arrows, chevrons, close are always proper SVGs.
SVG, not icon font.** Each icon ships as an SVG with `currentColor` stroke so it inherits text color.

Work Orders** — the hub. Each work order represents a repair job, broken into Lines (each with labor + parts + statuses like *Authorization Required*, *Authorized*, *Completed*). Every line can show/hide financial info (rate/margin/total).

Fonts**: Inter ships locally in `fonts/` across three optical sizes (18pt for UI, 24pt available for mid-size, 28pt for display). `colors_and_type.css` loads 18pt for the `Inter` family and 28pt as `Inter Display`. Nunito — which appeared only in a couple of Figma documentation labels — is no longer referenced; Inter covers all product UI.
Icons**: Lucide is used as a stand-in for Shopview's internal icon library (matched style).

Logo**: official wordmarks + symbols ship in `assets/` — `logo-primary-light.svg`, `logo-primary-dark.png`, `logo-black.svg`, `logo-white.svg`, `symbol-primary.svg`, `symbol-black.svg`, `symbol-white.svg`. Use the SVGs whenever possible; the dark-bg PNG is provided because the source uses raster effects the SVG export couldn't preserve.
Dara exploration screens** in Figma are work-in-progress, not canonical; the component pages (Buttons, Inputs, Badges, etc.) are the source of truth.
Schedule** — a week-view time grid where technicians' hours are blocked against work orders (e.g. "S1-8, ABC Truck Lines").
Customers** — customer records (e.g. *PepsiCo Foods Can...*) with contact, phone, IBS#.
Parts / Inventory** — parts catalog with bin location, category, supply, quantity.
Reports / Finance** — A/R Aging Detail, Canned Lines, Estimates, Invoicing.
`colors_and_type.css` — design tokens (colors, type, radii, shadows, spacing) as CSS variables, plus base element styles
`assets/` — logos, icon set references, logo SVG path

Shopview is **shop management software built for heavy-duty shops** — the people who service semi-trucks, tractors, trailers, fleet vehicles, and industrial equipment. The product is a web-based operations platform that runs the whole shop: work orders, schedule, customers, parts/inventory, technicians' timesheets, finance (estimates, invoicing, A/R), and reporting.
`fonts/` — web fonts (Inter, Nunito; both Google Fonts)
`preview/` — small sample cards that populate the Design System tab
`ui_kits/shopview-app/` — the primary product UI kit (React/JSX) with `index.html` demo + component library
ShopView copy is **direct, short, and verb-first**. It reads like a professional tool for busy shop managers — no marketing fluff, no friendliness performance.
Functional, not friendly.** The product is a system of record; copy gets out of the way.
Imperative verbs** dominate primary actions: *New Work Order*, *New Line*, *Authorize*, *Decline*, *Complete*, *New Inventory Part*. No "Let's…" or "Ready to…".

Domain language** is preferred over generic UI language. Say *Work Order*, *Line*, *Part*, *Bin Location*, *Service Advisor*, *Lead Technician*, *IBS#*, *VIN*, *Licence plate*, *Eng. Hr.*, *Milage* — not "item", "entry", "task".
Title Case for product-world nouns** (*Work Order*, *Part Returns*, *Canned Lines*, *A/R Aging Detail Report*) and in buttons and tabs (*New Work Order*, *My Work Orders*).
Sentence case for helper text and guidelines.** ("Use input fields only when the user must provide information, not for actions.")
No emoji** in product UI. (Guideline docs use ✅ ⚠️ ❌ informally to describe semantic color meaning, but the UI itself does not.)
First-person plural is avoided.** The product never refers to itself as "we". Users are addressed obliquely ("My Work Orders").
Status words are single tokens** — *Paid*, *Partially Paid*, *Unpaid*, *Awaiting*, *Requested*, *Authorized*, *Authorization Required*, *Approved*, *Completed*. They appear as badges.
Button labels: "Save", "Add Part", "Update", "New Work Order", "New Line", "New Inventory Part", "Authorize", "Decline", "Complete"
This design system is the source of truth for the product's look, feel, and language. It's derived directly from the official ShopView Design System Figma file.
Vague labels to avoid (per button guidelines): "OK", "New"
Preferred over generic: "Delete Part" not just "Delete"
Destructive action guideline: dedicated destructive style (red), used for delete/remove/reset.
Buttons trigger actions; links navigate. Never conflate.
One primary button per view. Never two primary buttons side by side.
Every button has states: Default, Hover, Focused, Disabled. Focused must be visible and accessible.
Always pair semantic colors with text or iconography — color alone never communicates state.
Error messages explain *what's wrong* and *how to fix it*.
Labels always visible; placeholders are examples, not substitutes for labels.

Shopview's palette is **a blue-led utilitarian system**: one strong action blue, a cool slate-grey ladder for structure, and four semantic colors for status. Additional colors (teal, cyan, violet, pink) are reserved for data/visualization contexts — not decoration.
Primary**: `#257CFF` (buttons, active tabs, links, logo accent). Pantone 2727 C.
Dark primary text**: `#364152` (grey-700 in our scale). Pantone 7546 C.
Neutrals (Grey)**: `#F8FAFC → #0F111A` — 11 steps. Used for layout, dividers, backgrounds, text. Grey-25–100 backgrounds, 200–400 containers/inputs, 500–700 text, 800–900 high-contrast/dark mode.
Never use grey for interactive elements except disabled.
Body text never lighter than Grey-500.
Badges paint background tint + darker text — they're pills, not solid chips.
Inter** is the single product typeface — body, labels, buttons, inputs, navigation, tables, and headlines. Chosen for tall x-height, open apertures, and clarity at small UI sizes.

Two optical sizes ship: **Inter 18pt** (aliased as `Inter`) for UI and body text, and **Inter 28pt** (aliased as `Inter Display`) for H1/H2 headlines where the tighter display cut reads better at large sizes.

Typescale: H1 30/38 (600 or 700), H2 24/32 semibold, H3 20/28 (500 or 700), H4 16/24 semibold, Body 1 14/20 (400/500/600), Body 2 12/16 (500/600, +1% letter-spacing), Caption 10/14 600 (+1.5% letter-spacing).
Import design-system components from 'index.js', not component internals.
Font not provided by the design system. Available: Inter, Inter Display.
Motion is utility, not personality. Hover lifts shadow. Press deepens fill. Focus glows. Nothing scales, nothing springs.
